title: Rutherford III — Irreversible
disclaimer: For professional education and simulation only. Not for direct patient-care decision-making.
synthetic_findings: Fixed mottling consistent with irreversible tissue injury

stages.title: Stage 1: Initial recognition and focused assessment
stages.narrative: A synthetic patient has a profoundly numb, immobile lower limb with fixed mottling. Neither arterial nor venous Doppler signals are audible.
stages.question: What is the most important initial educational interpretation?
stages.rationale: Profound anesthesia, paralysis or rigor, fixed mottling, and absent arterial and venous Doppler signals indicate irreversible tissue injury and a nonsalvageable limb.
stages.safety_principle: Recognizing irreversible ischemia prevents harmful attempts to reperfuse dead tissue and redirects attention to urgent senior and systemic assessment.

choices.text: Recognize probable irreversible ischemia and obtain urgent senior vascular-surgery assessment
choices.feedback: This identifies a nonsalvageable pattern and triggers urgent confirmation and systemic management.

choices.text: Assume the limb is Rutherford IIb and proceed directly to limb-salvage reperfusion
choices.feedback: Profound paralysis, anesthesia, fixed mottling, and absent venous flow exceed the findings of a salvageable IIb limb.

choices.text: Observe for spontaneous return of sensation before requesting senior vascular assessment
choices.feedback: Observation delays systemic and definitive management of a clinically irreversible presentation.

choices.text: Treat both absent Doppler signals as a technical limitation and disregard the neurological examination
choices.feedback: The neurological and skin findings independently support irreversible injury and cannot be dismissed as a Doppler artifact.

stages.title: Stage 2: Rutherford classification
stages.narrative: The synthetic limb has profound anesthesia, profound paralysis with rigor, fixed mottling, and absent arterial and venous Doppler signals.
stages.question: Which Rutherford category best matches these findings?
stages.rationale: Profound sensory and motor loss with absent arterial and venous Doppler signals defines Rutherford III irreversible ischemia, in which major tissue loss or permanent nerve damage is inevitable.
stages.safety_principle: A clearly irreversible limb is not a candidate for limb-salvage revascularization.

choices.text: Rutherford I — Viable
choices.feedback: A viable limb has no sensory or motor loss and retains audible arterial and venous Doppler signals.

choices.text: Rutherford IIa — Marginally threatened
choices.feedback: Rutherford IIa has no motor weakness and at most toe-limited sensory loss.

choices.text: Rutherford IIb — Immediately threatened
choices.feedback: Rutherford IIb remains salvageable and generally has mild-to-moderate weakness with preserved venous Doppler flow.

choices.text: Rutherford III — Irreversible
choices.feedback: The profound neurological loss, fixed tissue findings, and absent arterial and venous signals support Rutherford III.

stages.title: Stage 3: Immediate management
stages.narrative: Senior review is being arranged for the synthetic nonsalvageable limb. The patient requires stabilization and assessment for systemic effects of ischemic tissue.
stages.question: Which immediate management focus is most appropriate?
stages.rationale: Urgent senior vascular-surgery assessment should accompany analgesia, resuscitation, supportive care, and evaluation for hyperkalemia, acidosis, myoglobinuria, renal injury, hemodynamic deterioration, and systemic toxicity.
stages.safety_principle: The immediate priority is patient stabilization and systemic risk assessment, not an attempt to salvage a clinically nonviable limb.

choices.text: Obtain urgent senior vascular review, provide analgesia and resuscitation, and assess metabolic, renal, hemodynamic, and systemic consequences
choices.feedback: This addresses the patient-level risks created by irreversible ischemic tissue while definitive management is planned.

choices.text: Treat anticoagulation followed by immediate revascularization as the routine limb-salvage pathway
choices.feedback: A clearly irreversible limb should not undergo attempted limb-salvage reperfusion.

choices.text: Provide analgesia and arrange outpatient follow-up because the limb cannot be salvaged
choices.feedback: Irreversible limb ischemia carries urgent systemic and definitive-management risks and is not an outpatient presentation.

choices.text: Limit assessment to the limb and defer metabolic, renal, and hemodynamic evaluation
choices.feedback: Ischemic tissue can produce serious systemic consequences, so assessment cannot remain confined to the limb.

stages.title: Stage 4: Diagnostic imaging and treatment planning
stages.narrative: The synthetic examination is clinically consistent with irreversible Rutherford III ischemia, without uncertainty about limb viability.
stages.question: What is the best imaging and planning principle?
stages.rationale: When irreversibility is clinically established, anatomical imaging intended to plan limb-salvage revascularization offers no benefit and may delay definitive and systemic management.
stages.safety_principle: Do not allow unnecessary imaging to delay management of a clinically nonviable limb; limited investigation may be considered only if genuine diagnostic uncertainty would change the plan.

choices.text: Avoid imaging intended to plan limb-salvage reperfusion and proceed with definitive and systemic planning
choices.feedback: This avoids delay and an inappropriate salvage pathway when irreversibility is clinically established.

choices.text: Require computed tomographic angiography before analgesia, resuscitation, or senior discussion
choices.feedback: Imaging must not displace immediate supportive care and senior assessment.

choices.text: Perform angiography specifically to plan catheter-directed thrombolysis of the nonviable limb
choices.feedback: Thrombolytic limb salvage is inappropriate for clinically irreversible tissue.

choices.text: Use serial elective imaging to observe whether fixed mottling and paralysis improve
choices.feedback: Observation and serial imaging delay definitive management and do not reverse established tissue death.

stages.title: Stage 5: Definitive management and escalation
stages.narrative: Urgent senior assessment confirms that the synthetic limb is nonsalvageable and that attempted reperfusion would expose the patient to systemic risk.
stages.question: Which definitive-management direction is most appropriate?
stages.rationale: Primary amputation or appropriate palliation should be considered according to physiological condition, operative suitability, prognosis, and goals of care; a specific amputation level requires individualized assessment.
stages.safety_principle: Reperfusing a nonviable limb can release potassium, acid, myoglobin, and other ischemic metabolites, causing renal injury, hemodynamic collapse, and systemic toxicity.

choices.text: Plan primary amputation or appropriate palliation according to physiology, operative suitability, prognosis, and goals of care
choices.feedback: This recognizes the nonsalvageable limb while individualizing the definitive direction without prescribing an amputation level.

choices.text: Attempt surgical or endovascular revascularization before considering amputation in every case
choices.feedback: Routine reperfusion of a clearly irreversible limb offers no salvage benefit and may cause severe systemic harm.

choices.text: Specify the same exact amputation level for every Rutherford III presentation
choices.feedback: Amputation level depends on individualized tissue, anatomical, physiological, and rehabilitation assessment.

choices.text: Continue supportive care indefinitely without discussing amputation, palliation, prognosis, or goals of care
choices.feedback: Supportive care must be paired with a timely definitive plan and appropriate goals-of-care discussion.
